commitments.text: Commitment to a manned access gate at the O'Donnel River north of Mt. McMaster. This commitment, coupled with specifying that the Tulsequah Chief Road is a private industrial road and the associated prohibition of all non-legitimate land or resource tenure holder use, should mitigate impacts of increased human access south of the O'Donnel River.
Commitment to implement a no-firearms and no-hunting policy for all mine employees and contractors during all phases of construction and operation.

Commitment to undertake detailed habitat inspection as part of the Follow-up and Monitoring Program beginning in May 1998. The proponent has further agreed that this detailed assessment would provide the basis for assessment of off-site habitat compensation, should it be required. The identification of important habitat patches is necessary at a resolution of 1:20,000 map scale or larger.

Commitment to avoid important habitats for all species as part of the terms-of-reference for the independent Environmental Supervision Plan. The proponent has verbally committed to hiring three Environment Supervisors to work with ministry staff to provide detailed on-site evaluation of important habitat areas at a finer scale.

The proponent has addressed the relative merits of DNA hair analysis versus track counts for inventory and monitoring grizzly bear populations. The proponent accepted the concept of adopting the DNA method if / when it is proven, and agrees with the proposed “phase in” recommendation respecting DNA hair analysis.

Commitment to provide off-site compensation for direct loss of wildlife habitats during operation of the mine, and any residual loss of habitat resulting from ineffectiveness of reclamation measures, that are identified as project development procedures in consultation with MELP.

Prior to the issuance of waste management permits the proponent shall, to the satisfaction of the Regional Manager, Environmental Protection, Ministry of Environment, Lands and Parks, Smithers, provide acceptable plans and programs to address the commitments and requirements described in the Environmental Effects Monitoring (EEM) Outline. The EEM Outline includes further baseline data collection for Shazah Slough and key high value fish habitats associated with the proposed access road (water quality, sediment and aquatic life; groundwater quality and hydrology in the predicted tailings pond seepage zone) and specification of a detailed EEM program for the road and minesite.

Watercourse crossings must be constructed to ensure no impediment to upstream fish migration. Fish habitat values at the Boyer Creek crossing cannot be maintained unless a clear-span bridge is used for the crossing; DFO and MELP both indicate satisfaction with the proposed use of clear-span bridges.

The proponent has developed a groundwater pumping contingency which includes new groundwater monitoring wells and additional baseline work on Shazah Slough outlined in the EEM proposal as proposed in the Bruce Geotechnical Reports. Identify contingency mitigation and demonstrate effectiveness on predicted seepage quality.

The reagent chemicals must be stored in secure areas that are a discrete section of the plant site containment system. Fuel areas must have concrete spill contingency basins that will collect and contain volume maximums at all tank locations. The proponent should conduct risk assessment activities to identify how and where fuel/chemical spills could occur throughout the project area for all development and operational phases, and establish written fuel/chemical storage handling procedures.

If archaeological material is inadvertently encountered during construction, all work must cease and the Archaeology Branch must be contacted. A Heritage Conservation Act Section 12 permit will be required for road construction which will affect the three recorded trails.

The degree of risk associated with seepages of tailings pond water into Shazah Slough is governed by inputs to the tailings pond. This dictates that inputs occur according to a set of criteria which will guarantee acceptable volumes of high quality (low concentrations of contaminants) seepage. These criteria will be established as part of the Waste Management Act Permit associated with the discharge to the tailings pond.

2.  To detect changes in the size of the grizzly bear population (relative abundance) and/or changes in the trends of several population

Habitat and displacement- related objectives are described in the CEA (Habitat and Displacement submodels), the Project Report 
(Terrestrial Ecosystem Mapping interpretations), or the fiheries (salmon) monitoring plan.
METHODS
Phase I – The term of the grizzly bear cumulative effects analysis
Phase I of the grizzly bear monitoring plan will be from the present (January 1998) to the end of the 2-year term of the grizzly bear 
cumulative effects analysis (see MacHutchon 1998). During this time, grizzly bear monitoring activities will:
1.  Detect short-term changes in grizzly bear populations (relative abundance) and changes in several population trend indices;

3.  Allow for a critical evaluation of the monitoring protocols and trend indices proposed here. Phase I will conclude with 
recommendations for monitoring protocols to be implemented during phase II of the monitoring plan, e.g., If track surveys can be 
shown to be as effective as hair capture and DNA analysis for detecting grizzly bear population changes then track surveys may be 
recommended as the main monitoring protocol for phase II;
4.  Provide population ecology information for use in the cumulative effects analysis (e.g., the average number of cubs per litter)

5.  Determine yearly changes in direct grizzly bear mortality. 
Phase I of the grizzly bear monitoring plan consists of 2 parts:

1. Strengthen the grizzly bear monitoring program as outlined in the Tulsequah Chief Project report (Rescan 1997, Vol. IV, section 7.2.6) 
as follows:
a) Track surveys — Many attempts have been made to relate the amount of sign observed per unit effort to the relative abundance of 
bears (Manning et al. 1994). Track counts may be useful for detecting long-term population trends, but large changes in population size 
are probably necessary before the change would be detected. To make track survey counts most effective for monitoring grizzly bear 
populations:
i) the specific protocol of the track count surveys and the statistical approach to making use of track survey data should be 
reviewed by a quantitative ecologist,
ii) track surveys should be conducted under comparable conditions each year,
iii) time surveys to coincide with the peak of spawning. Salmon numbers can fluctuate yearly and availability to bears can 
be affected by changes in water level and clarity,
iv) measure yearly changes in salmon abundance and availability,
v) sample sizes have to be large when stream use by bears is low to detect statistically significant differences between two 
indices.
vi) make sure track counts are done over a consistent area of substrate,
vii) attempt to account for multiple track sets by the same bear, 
viii) the actual relationship between the track count index and population size needs to be tested. Some calibration with 
another population estimator would be needed to at least determine the nature of the relationship (i.e., linear or non-linear) 
(see hair capture and DNA analysis below).
b) Incidental Observations — Incidental observations of grizzly bears are only useful as a monitoring technique if the effort expended to 
get the information is consistent and sufficient enough to ensure adequate sample sizes. A systematic approach similar to that used to 
monitor populations in the U.S. (Servheen 1993 & 1997) should be used as an alternative to simply recording “incidental observations”. 
The U.S. system has been developed to monitor three key parameters: 1) the number of unduplicated females with cubs seen annually, 2) 
the distribution of females with young or family groups throughout the ecosystem, and 3) the annual number of known human-caused 
mortalities (Servheen 1993). Servheen (1997) reviewed the efficacy of these monitoring approaches compared to newer techniques

2. Grizzly bear hair capture and DNA analysis techniques for estimating relative abundance should be done to make the monitoring plan 
more consistent with current B.C. Resources Inventory Committee standards (RIC 1997). A maximum likelihood estimator (MLE) for 
cumulative counts can be adapted for estimating population size based on the accumulation of unique bears at hair capture sites (Boyce et 
al. 1998 in Servheen 1997). Relative abundance population estimates should be done in the best groupings of grizzly bear habitats at the 
lower elevations of each of the following 3 ecosection and biogeoclimatic zone combinations, Coastal Western Hemlock (CWH) zone of 
the Boundary Ranges (BOR) ecosection, Subboreal Spruce (SBS) zone of the Taltan Highland (THH) ecosection, and Boreal White and 
Black Spruce (BWBS) zone of the Teslin Plateau (TEP) ecosection.
Phase II – From the end of the grizzly bear CEA to the end of the life of the Tulsequah 
Chief Project
Phase II of the grizzly bear monitoring plan will be from the end of the 2-year term of the grizzly bear cumulative effects analysis (see 
MacHutchon 1998) to the end of the life of the Tulsequah Chief Project. During this time, grizzly bear monitoring activities will:

1.  Maintain a co-operative arrangement between Redfern Resources Ltd., the B.C. government, the Taku River Tlingit First Nation, 
and other local residents in the monitoring of grizzly bear populations;

3.  Determine yearly changes in direct grizzly bear mortality. 
Phase II of the grizzly bear monitoring plan will use the recommended protocols arising out of phase I to continue to monitor grizzly bear 
populations over the life of the Tulsequah Chief Project.

●     changes in animal numbers that may be a consequence of the development can be isolated from those that are a result of natural

4. To determine changes in selected demographic parameters. Total counts or stratified random block surveys of selected herds near the 
Tulsequah Chief mine and mine access road will be conducted such that:
●     herd productivity can be measured on an annual basis (calf survival and recruitment); 
●     estimates of natural mortality levels can be evaluated.

5. To quantify ungulate mortalities along the Tulsequah Chief Mine Access road. The use of a permanently manned game check (for 
recording vehicle-collisions and hunter kills), compulsory inspection (sheep, goats and caribou), and interviews with hunters will ensure 
that:
●     all human-caused mortalities are within acceptable limits (species specific); 
●     the spatial distribution of human-caused mortalites and hunting effort is not area-concentrated; 
●     the current human mortality levels are consistent with historic information (caribou only); 
●     estimates of wounding, illegal killing and crippling losses can be evaluated. 
GENERAL METHODOLOGY
Seasonal Distribution:
Seasonal distribution is monitored by a radio-collar/telemetry program. A randomly-selected sample of approximately 20 - 25 animals 
will be captured and radio-collared. The number of animals selected is based on a relative sample size according to current population 
estimates. Twenty to twenty-five animals is a tractable sample size that is easily handled, provides manageable data, accounts for natural 
mortality and collar attrition and may allow a statistical measure of confidence in the data. An acceptable sample for caribou (500), 
moose (1400) and goats (400?) will be 25 collars each. An acceptable sample size for sheep will be dependent upon the number of sheep 
found during survey flights.
Monitoring of the collared animals (relocation) is conducted through telemetry using a fixed-wing aircraft throughout the year. Frequency 
of relocation is based upon movement of the animals i.e. during spring, summer, fall, twice per month may be adequate and during 
calving or rut seasons once per week may be required. Likewise during the winter months when movement is reduced, once per month 
may be adequate.
Helicopter telemetry to be conducted with specifics as follows:
June: for determination of calving grounds and calving success/herd productivity
October/November: for determination of rutting locations/herd productivity
March: for determination of winter locations and yearling mortality/herd productivity
As telemetry proceeds, movement of species between summer and winter ranges, to preferred calving grounds and preferred rutting areas 
in relation to the road corridor and traffic will be detected.
Wildlife Population Surveys:
Population estimates will follow current B.C. Resources Inventory Committee standards. For ungulates see RIC (1997a & 1997b).

2. Total Counts:
are aerial surveys (RIC 1997a) which occur in discrete blocks of relatively open upland habitat. Habitat areas are mapped into blocks 
which could encompass an entire mountain. Aerial surveys are conducted circularly, at progressive elevations, until the upland habitat 
has been thoroughly searched.
Total count surveys for caribou are conducted during the rut when the probability of herd concentration is highest. Mountain goat total 
counts are conducted during the summer when visibility is optimum. Thin-horn sheep total counts are conducted during late winter prior 
to dispersal to summer range.
Wildlife population surveys will focus on areas potentially influenced by the Tulsequah Chief mine and mine access road. Specific 
locations are as follows:
Caribou: Yukon border to the east side of Atlin Lake to the west side of Teslin Lake and to the northern Nakina watershed/O’Donnel 
River; Spruce Creek to Silver Salmon River including Johnson to Laurie Ranges, Mount McMaster, Chikoida Mountain, Focus 
Mountain, O’Keefe Upland for calving and rutt; Spruce and Wilson Creek valleys,O’Donnel, Pike and Silver Salmon River valleys for 
winter range.
Moose: Yukon border to the east side of Atlin Lake to the west side of Teslin Lake and to the northern Nakina watershed/O’Donnel 
River; Spruce Creek to Silver Salmon River including Johnson to Laurie Ranges, Mount McMaster, Chikoida Mountain, Focus 
Mountain, O’Keefe Upland; Sloko River, Lower Nakonake River and Tulsequah River drainages.
Goat: Focus and Chikoida Mountains, Sloko River, upper Nakonake River and Shazah Creek Valley, Mount Sparling and Mount 
Manville.
Sheep: O’Keefe and Focus Mountains
